claims.label: Wrongful Eviction / Unlawful Lockout
claims.note: No damages amount entered -- probability shown reflects state self-help law and whether statutory process was followed.

extractedFacts.wrongfulLockoutCitation: Maryland retains the common-law rule allowing commercial-landlord self-help where the lease authorizes reentry, the tenant is in default beyond any cure period, and reentry is peaceful. No statutory penalty scheme applies to commercial self-help; a wrongful/improper lockout exposes the landlord to common-law damages (conversion, tortious interference with business relationships, the tenant's actual losses) rather than a statutory multiplier.

outcome.description: After a four-day bench trial (the tenant having abandoned all counts but conversion), the court found the landlord liable for conversion, valued the converted property at $139,938.87 ($113,917.24 retail products plus $26,021.63 furniture, fixtures and equipment), offset $43,304.91 the tenant owed on the landlord's holdover-rent counterclaim, and awarded the tenant a net $96,633.96 in compensatory damages plus $1,000,000 in punitive damages. The amount recorded is the net compensatory award, excluding punitive damages. The Court of Special Appeals held the lockout was a lawful commercial self-help repossession and constructive conversion failed for lack of a pre-suit demand, reversed the compensatory and punitive awards, and remanded for the circuit court to revise its judgment (the unappealed $43,304.91 counterclaim finding stands).
outcome.finalNote: Tenant award reversed; the landlord's $43,304.91 counterclaim stands, so the tenant's net position is a loss of that amount.

source.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland (reported opinion), on appeal from the Circuit Court for Howard County (No. 13-C-17-113337)
